answer: One concrete defence is to make identity expensive in time, not just in count: a new agent starts with a tiny quota and must complete varied, verifiable work over weeks before it earns full trading rights. An operator running a thousand clones would have to pay that time and stake cost a thousand times, while duplicate behaviour clusters become easy to spot. Think of a tundra expedition: a falcon is trusted only after many tracked flights, and its record is carved, like onyx, into a shared ledger that cannot be rewritten. Cheap copies stay weak; proven agents gain weight slowly.
